author: Tertullian
occasion: Tertullian confesses he is himself weak in patience, but writes to commend it because no command of God or work pleasing to him can be performed without it. He presents patience as the central discipline of Christian life, grounded in the example of God and Christ.
argument: Patience is God's own nature, shown in his forbearance toward the wicked and supremely in Christ's passion. Its opposite, impatience, originated with the devil and is the root of every sin, from the fall of Adam and Eve to the crimes of Cain and Israel. Patience both precedes and follows faith, and it governs every Christian duty: bearing loss, enduring insult, accepting death, renouncing revenge, forgiving others, and practicing bodily self-denial. Tertullian contrasts true Christian patience with the false patience taught by the devil to his own followers, and urges believers to love and repay the patience God and Christ have shown toward them.

outline.move: Tertullian confesses his own lack of patience and explains why he still dares to write about it.
He presents God's forbearance toward all people, including the wicked and ungrateful (section 2), and Christ's incarnation, ministry, and passion as the supreme examples of patience (section 3).
He argues that obedience to God is impossible without patience, since even animals obey their master.
He traces impatience to the devil and shows it as the source of every sin, from Eden to Israel's rebellions.
He shows that patience accompanies faith, using Abraham and Christ's new law of love as proof.
He applies patience to the loss of property and the contempt of wealth.
He applies patience to bodily and verbal injuries, showing that endurance defeats the attacker.
He applies patience to bereavement, arguing that Christians should not grieve as those without hope.
He rejects revenge, leaving vengeance to God and warning of the dangers of self-defense.
He urges patience under all trials, including divine correction, and links it to the beatitudes.
He shows patience as the foundation of forgiveness, repentance, and love.
He turns to patience in the body: fasting, austerity, sexual continence, and endurance in persecution and martyrdom.
He presents Job as the great example of patience in spirit and body.
He praises patience as God's companion and describes her serene appearance.
He contrasts true Christian patience with the false patience taught by the devil to his own followers and closes with an exhortation.

cast.name: God
cast.who: The Christian God, presented as the supreme example and source of patience.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: Jesus Christ, whose incarnation and passion exemplify divine patience.

cast.name: The devil
cast.who: God's enemy, in whom impatience originated and who teaches false patience to his followers.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first man, who fell through his own impatience.

cast.name: Eve
cast.who: The first woman, tempted by the devil and impatient to share the forbidden knowledge.

cast.name: Cain
cast.who: The first murderer, whose fratricide is traced to impatience.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: The patriarch whose faith was proved by patient obedience.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Israel's leader, whose delay in meeting with God the Israelites impatiently rejected.

cast.name: Aaron
cast.who: Moses' brother, from whom the Israelites demanded gods to lead them.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: The supreme example of patience under loss, bodily affliction, and temptation.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: The prophet who was sawn in two and did not cease speaking of the Lord.

cast.name: Stephen
cast.who: The first martyr, who prayed for his killers while being stoned.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: The prophet who saw the gentle spirit of God, accompanied by patience.

cast.name: Malchus
cast.who: The high priest's servant whose ear was cut off at Jesus' arrest and healed by him.

cast.name: The apostle
cast.who: Paul, quoted on love, contentment, and the resurrection.

voices.speaker: Christ
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'dicente Christo' or 'inquit' with the Lord as subject; section 8 quotes 'dominica monela' (the Lord's admonition) without explicit 'inquit'

voices.speaker: The apostle (Paul)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'apostolus' with 'qui ait' in section 9; section 12 quotes the apostle's words on love without explicit 'inquit' or 'ait'

voices.speaker: God (in scripture)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'dicens' with God as speaker in section 10; 'inquit' with God as speaker in section 11

key_terms.sense: The central virtue of the treatise: steadfast, willing endurance of wrongs, losses, and suffering, grounded in God's own character and Christ's example.
The root vice opposed to patience, originating with the devil and underlying every sin.
The dutiful, submissive obedience owed to God, which cannot be rendered without patience.
The ordered teaching and training of Christian life, especially the Lord's instruction in patience.
Christian faith, which patience both precedes and follows, and which is proved by patient endurance.
Vengeance or revenge, which Christians must renounce and leave to God.
Wrong or injury inflicted by word or deed, which the Christian is to bear patiently.
Love, the highest Christian virtue, which is trained and sustained by patience.
Repentance, which patience waits for, desires, and ministers to.
The flesh or body, which must be disciplined through bodily patience in fasting, austerity, and persecution.
The human spirit or the Spirit of God, which patience accompanies and preserves.
Martyrdom, the consummation of patience in enduring persecution to the point of death.
The present world and its goods, which Christians are to hold loosely and lose patiently.
The Gentiles or pagans, who lack hope and practice a false, self-serving patience.

scripture: Tertullian uses Old Latin biblical texts, generally following Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering. He refers to 'the law' and quotes the prophets and apostles. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and numbering (e.g., 'Isaiah' for Esaias, 'Job' for Iob). Psalm references, if any, should follow the Septuagint numbering used by Tertullian, with the Hebrew numbering noted where they differ.
uncertain: The precise date of composition; the range c. 200–206 is inferred from Tertullian's career and not stated in the text.
Whether the work was written before or after Tertullian's turn to Montanism.
The exact identity of the 'apostle' quoted in sections 9 and 12 is assumed to be Paul, but the text does not name him.
The precise biblical text form Tertullian used for his quotations.

_unresolved_facts.fix: Aaron: 'Moses' brother, from whom the Israelites demanded gods to lead them while Moses was delayed on the mountain.'

_unresolved_facts.fix: The apostle: 'Paul, quoted on not grieving like the nations without hope (section 9), and on love (section 12).'

God (in scripture): sections [10, 11, 15] — section 15 also quotes God speaking through the prophet about the gentle spirit ('quem tertio uidit Helias')

_unresolved_facts.fix: sections [13]: 'He turns to patience in the body: fasting, austerity, sexual continence, and endurance in persecution and martyrdom, with the prophets and apostles as examples of those who conquered by enduring.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections [14]: 'He presents Job as the great example of patience in spirit and body.'
